title: Bhajiya: How to Make the Perfect Assorted Indian Fritters at Home
excerpt: A step-by-step guide to making crisp, golden mixed bhajiya — the classic Indian street snack of batter-fried potato, brinjal, chilli, and bread.
body:
• Bhajiya are crisp Indian fritters made by coating thin vegetable slices in a seasoned gram flour batter and deep-frying — a staple street food across Gujarat and Maharashtra.
  • A mixed bhajiya platter typically includes potato, brinjal (eggplant), large green chillies, and bread, each fried separately for distinct textures.
  • The batter uses gram flour (besan) with rice flour for extra crispness, seasoned with carom seeds (ajwain), asafoetida, turmeric, and red chilli powder.
  • Served hot with green chutney and masala chai, bhajiya are the quintessential Indian monsoon snack and a fixture at street food stalls and home kitchens alike.

Few Indian snacks carry the emotional weight of bhajiya. The sound of vegetables hitting hot oil, the aroma of gram flour and ajwain, the first crisp bite dipped in green chutney — for millions of Indians, this is the taste of monsoon evenings, chai-time conversations, and festive gatherings. And while the names change across regions — bajji in the south, pakora in the north, bhaji in Maharashtra — the fundamental pleasure of batter-fried vegetables remains universal.

A definitive recipe from Dassana Amit of Veg Recipes of India lays out the technique for a mixed bhajiya platter, the kind sold at street food stalls and farsan shops across Gujarat and Maharashtra. Unlike mixed vegetable pakoras that combine chopped vegetables in a single batter, this approach coats individual vegetable slices and fries each variety separately, producing distinct textures on one plate.

The Batter

The foundation is two cups of gram flour (besan) mixed with a third cup of rice flour, which provides the characteristic shatteringly crisp coating. Carom seeds (ajwain) add their distinctive thyme-like warmth, while asafoetida (hing), turmeric, and red chilli powder round out the seasoning. Some cooks add a pinch of baking soda for puffiness, though Dassana notes that thorough whisking aerates the batter enough to produce a light coating without it.

Consistency is everything. The batter needs to be thick enough to cling to vegetable slices without sliding off, yet thin enough to flow from a whisk. "If it is too thick, add a little more water. If it becomes thin, mix in a small amount of gram flour," she advises. A test drop of batter in the oil should rise gradually to the surface without browning too quickly.

The Platter

The traditional assortment includes four components, each offering a different eating experience. Thinly sliced potatoes produce a chip-like crunch. Brinjal (eggplant) slices, soaked beforehand in salted water to remove bitterness and prevent discoloration, turn tender and creamy inside their golden shell. Large green chillies, slit lengthwise and deseeded, deliver a gentle warmth. Bread triangles, quickly dipped and fried, become crisp and pillowy.

Each ingredient requires slightly different handling. The brinjal slices must be patted completely dry before coating, or the oil will splutter and the batter won't adhere. The bread should be dipped and fried immediately — letting it sit in the batter turns it soggy. And the chillies need mild, large varieties specifically suited for bhajiya, not the small, fiery ones that would overpower the dish.

The Frying Technique

Deep-frying in a kadai (Indian wok) over medium heat is the traditional method. Oil temperature management separates good bhajiya from greasy ones — too cool and the fritters absorb oil, too hot and the coating browns before the vegetables cook through. Frying in small batches prevents overcrowding that drops the oil temperature.

"Maintain a medium to medium-high oil temperature throughout frying. Allow the oil to become hot again between batches if its temperature drops."

— Dassana Amit, Veg Recipes of India

Finished bhajiya are drained on kitchen paper and optionally sprinkled with chaat masala and chopped coriander before serving. They pair traditionally with coriander chutney, pudina chutney, or tamarind chutney alongside a cup of masala chai — a combination that no Indian household needs to be told about.

Variations and Dietary Notes

The platter can be customized with cauliflower florets, capsicum strips, raw banana rounds, or onion rings substituted for or added to the standard four. For a gluten-free version, the bread is simply omitted and gluten-free asafoetida used, since the gram flour and rice flour base is naturally gluten-free.

Bhajiya are best eaten immediately, when the coating is at peak crispness. Leftovers can be refrigerated for a day and reheated in an oven or air fryer at 180°C — never a microwave, which turns the coating chewy. But truthfully, leftover bhajiya are a rare phenomenon in any Indian household.
